section_summaries.epidemiology: The disease is reported from the United States to Argentina, including Caribbean islands, and travelers to endemic areas can present with the disease on their return. It affects both adults and children, often predominantly pediatric in some areas. In temperate areas of southern Brazil, transmission is focal and seasonal (spring/summer), with a low lethality rate (1.3%-7.4%).
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Abdominal angiostrongyliasis is caused by Angiostrongylus costaricensis, a filariform nematode that normally lives within the mesenteric arteries of rodents (definitive hosts). Humans become infected by ingesting slugs or food items contaminated with mollusks or their secretions. The adult worms in the mesenteric arteries induce thrombosis and tissue necrosis, while eggs, embryos, larvae, and excretion-secretion products trigger inflammatory reactions. Pathologically, there is a hardened, thickened intestinal wall, reduced lumen, and potential perforation. Histopathology reveals heavy eosinophilic infiltration, including eosinophilic arteritis, granulomatous reactions, and the presence of eggs, embryos, and larvae. Extra-intestinal lesions include eggs and embryos in mesenteric lymph nodes (causing reticuloendothelial hyperplasia and eosinophilic infiltration) and hepatic parenchyma.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Patients typically complain of pain in the right iliac fossa and right flank, often with painful palpation and rectal examination. Fever (38-38.5°C) is common, sometimes accompanied by chills, and can persist for weeks in chronic cases. Anorexia, vomiting, and constipation are present in about half the patients. A tumor-like mass may be palpable in the right lower quadrant. Leukocytosis (15,000-50,000/mm³) and eosinophilia (20-50%, up to 91%) are frequent. Extra-intestinal findings include right upper quadrant pain, enlarged and tender liver with yellowish granulomas, and testicular involvement leading to acute pain, redness, and purple discoloration, often misdiagnosed as testicular torsion.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis relies on characteristic features and an appropriate exposure history, often mimicking appendicitis. Imaging can reveal suggestive findings in the terminal ileum, cecum, appendix, and ascending colon, with intestinal wall thickening resembling colon carcinoma. Eggs and larvae are not typically found in stools. Antibody detection by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in tissue samples are available at reference laboratories.
section_summaries.treatment: Surgery is sometimes necessary, though increasingly, cases are followed without it as the disease can be self-limiting. There is currently no specific anti-parasitic drug therapy, as clinical trials are lacking. In vitro and in vivo studies suggest anti-parasitic drugs can excite parasites, leading to erratic migrations and worsened lesions, thus chemotherapy is not recommended.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention involves avoiding the ingestion of slugs and raw food or water that may be contaminated with slugs or their secretions. Disinfection of vegetables using a 1.5% bleach solution is recommended.
